doc.title: Byron Stripling interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 25, 1998 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Parents' worry about a musician's income and a week of studio work
summary: He explains that musicians carry their own pension and health coverage, tells students their parents are right until proven wrong, and describes a solo jingle session.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Advice to young musicians starting out

blocks.x: So but look, Monk, if you don’t understand that concept of, well maybe I’m not working for three days, four days, five days. Maybe I don’t work for a week and a half. If you’ve been used to nine to five, see, us musicians here, and so few of us talk about it — and I make it my job to talk to students about it that want to go into music — so many of us — I’m not on a specific pension plan, I have to take that responsibility myself. I’m not on any college payroll for a health plan. I have to take that responsibility myself. So my parents didn’t understand that. And I always tell kids, how many of you have been told by your parents you shouldn’t go into music, just do this for fun, you’ll enjoy it, it’s great, but you need to get a real job. And usually I get sixty percent of the people say that when I’m speaking to people that are aspiring musicians. And I say you know what? Your parents are absolutely right, until you can prove them wrong. And that means that you have to then get ammunition and you have to be able to say well this is what I will do as a musician. These are the opportunities. And so one of the first things I do is have them make a list of everything you could do in music. And what I can do is sometimes I’ll give them an average week for myself. This Monday I’m going to play a jingle for Jolly Jelly or some kind of thing like that, where I’ll go in, I won’t see the music ahead of time. Most times in the 21st century, that’s my catch word, you’re the only person in the studio. I usually go in by myself, and this particular company I’m working for I’m

usually the only trumpet player there, they’ve already pre-recorded the track, and they’re going to be like Byron play, here’s some music, play this on top of it. Sometimes I’ll go improvise something on top of it. Sometimes they won’t want anything close to improvisation. Sometimes it’ll be classically oriented. Sometimes they’ll want the flugelhorn. It has to be very well in tune, playing with a synthesizer is very different in playing because the synthesizer is right on the pitch, which means I’ve got to pull out because we tend to play a little sharp as brass players and try to get a little edge. We play a little bit, just a little bit — so you have to adjust differently. There’s all those things. You wouldn’t want me to play flat, would you?
